newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha travels south to seek support.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha travels south to seek support.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha, eager to drum up the flagging support of his people, is preparing to tour the country's south to press home his message that only his right-wing government can help them ease their plight.

Hundreds of thousands of Albanians lost their hard-earned life savings after a string of shady pyramid investment schemes failed last month, sparking five weeks of nationwide popular protest and violent unrest.

Eager to counter accusations that his Democratic Party government looked on while the schemes spread and failed to warn the public of their dangers, Berisha has criss-crossed the country to deliver a series of speeches to his supporters.

Sources close to his office said he was expected to travel to Fiere, some 110 km (70 miles) south of the capital Tirana, on Sunday. Albania's relatively prosperous southern region has been hit hardest by the collapse of the funds, which relied on new money to pay sky-high interest rates due on older deposits.

In the northern town of Shkoder he told a boisterous crowd of 4,000 on Saturday that the opposition Socialists, reformed heirs to the Communists, were exploiting the crisis which has engulfed Europe's poorest nation in a bid to regain power.
"The communists thought it was the right time to swallow Albanian democracy but we will never allow them to take power again," he told the cheering crowd.
The key opposition Socialists changed their name from the Communist Party after Albania emerged from 45 years of ruthless Stalinist isolation in 1990.
"We are sure it was not investors who set fires to public buildings last month but the (former) communists and secret police who want to take power through violence," he said.

Several town halls were set on fire by angry crowds across Albania's south last month. In the Adriatic port town of Vlore, three protesters died and 150 were injured in pitched battles between angry investors and police two weeks ago.

In Vlore, which has spearheaded the opposition to the rule of Berisha and Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government, some 7,000 demonstraters turned out for an 18th day to stage a noisy street march.
The leader of the Social Democrats, now allied with the Socialists in a cross-party opposition forum, told protesters the government should resign over its handling of the scandal.
"Students said "No" to the communist dictatorship in 1990, Vlore students will say "No" to the Berisha dictatorship," said Skender Gjinushi.

Democratic Party deputies from Vlore, which last week came out in support of opposition calls for Meksi's resignation, have called for an extraordinary session of parliament to discuss the situation in the town, state television reported.

Top members of the Democrats met behind closed doors on Saturday to discuss the scandal, which has become the most serious crisis since Berisha and Meksi came to power in 1992 on promises of economic growth and rising living standards.
Both have vigorously defended their record and say there is no chance of them relinquishing power now.
Officials estimate Albanians sank $1 to $2 billion in the fraudulent schemes. In the final frenzy, thousands of people also sold homes, property or valuables to pump more money into the pyramids.
